title: Governor Bush’s Article Trust in Education Has Fallen
author: Douglas Carnine
summary: Douglas Carnine responds to Jeb Bush's argument in The 74 that trust in education has fallen, agreeing that teachers must be empowered and that accountability is essential. He defines empowerment as giving teachers a coherent knowledge base, quality materials, effective preparation and orderly classrooms, citing the Nick Gibb and Robert Peal account of England's gains from synthetic phonics, knowledge-rich curricula, explicit instruction and aligned accountability. He then presents the Evidence Advocacy Center's five pillars for evidence-based professions: a shared knowledge base, evidence-aligned preparation, meaningful licensure and development, rigorous accreditation, and systemic accountability. His central claim is that accountability must apply to the whole system and not just to classroom teachers, with a coalition he calls the Collaborative of the Harmed to press for transparency. He parts company with Bush on one point, saying righting the ship is in fact rocket science. The piece is partly an advocacy statement for the author's own organisation, so readers should weigh it accordingly.
points: Teacher empowerment means supplying a coherent knowledge base, strong materials, effective preparation and supportive leadership, not leaving teachers to navigate conflicting theories alone.
The author attributes England's improvement to synthetic phonics, knowledge-rich curricula, explicit instruction, high expectations, aligned assessment and system-level accountability.
The Evidence Advocacy Center proposes five pillars borrowed from evidence-based professions, spanning knowledge base, preparation, licensure, accreditation and accountability.

Accountability should reach state agencies, preparation programs, accreditors, licensure boards and districts, with corrective accountability for those who ignore evidence and constructive accountability for those never equipped.
He disputes the claim that reform is not rocket science, citing Louisa Moats on the difficulty of teaching reading, and calls for pressure from families, employers and colleges.
quotes: This is the central weakness in much American reform. We often demand better results from teachers without ensuring that preparation programs, state agencies, districts, licensure systems, and instructional program providers have given them the knowledge and tools needed to succeed.

For Governor Bush, empowerment does not mean leaving teachers alone to navigate conflicting theories, weak curricula, inadequate preparation, and constantly changing initiatives. It means giving them a coherent knowledge base, high-quality materials, effective preparation, useful professional development, supportive leadership, and orderly classrooms.
England’s experience suggests that accountability works best when educators have access to effective practices and coherent instructional systems.

Educators who have been informed about what works but fail to apply it require corrective accountability. Those who were never adequately prepared and supported require constructive accountability with better training, instructional resources, and professional support.
While teachers are the most visible participants in education, they do not control many of the conditions affecting their performance.

The education system rarely holds itself accountable. Ineffective practices persist because of institutional inertia, weak oversight, ideology, or adherence to educational trends unsupported by research.
Together, these groups can demand transparency, independent evidence audits, and accountability across the entire education system—not merely at the classroom level.

In his article, Governor Bush asserted, “Righting this ship isn’t rocket science.” I agree with Governor Bush’s prescription to empower teachers; however, I think righting the ship is, in fact, rocket science.
